name: Every Storey the Same

severity_by_style.why: The graduation is what makes the front sit on the ground rather than float; it is invisible in plan and fatal in elevation.
The style graduates harder than any other - 8 to 15 per cent per storey off an 11-14 ft first floor - so equal storeys destroy it outright.
As Georgian, and Federal attenuation depends on it.
The frieze-band attic makes its own extreme graduation, and the two-storey block below is often nearly equal.
One or one and a half storeys; there is usually no second full storey to graduate.
Ceiling heights are differentiated by function rather than by storey.
The skin runs across storey lines and suppresses the reading of storeys altogether.

symptom: First and second storeys the same height, first- and second-floor windows the same unit, and a front that consequently floats. The building has no base and no diminution; it reads as two identical layers stacked, and the cornice sits on top of the upper layer with nothing about the composition explaining why the building stops there.

cause.explanation: Framing lumber arrives as precut studs at 92 5/8, 104 5/8 and 116 5/8 in, and the whole house is framed from one length because a second length is a second delivery, a second stack and a second chance to cut the wrong one. Drywall comes in 8, 9 and 10 ft sheets. Windows are ordered as a single unit type across both floors to reach a volume price break and to reduce the schedule to one line. Every one of those pushes toward identical storeys, and none of them ever appears on a drawing as a decision anyone made.
cause.cost_saved: $1,500-4,000 on a 2,500 sf house in ordering, cutting and waste across a single stud length and a single window type.

rule_violated.statement: The second storey is 0.85 of the first, storey to storey, including the floor structure; a half storey or attic is 0.62 of the floor below.
The second storey stands to the first as 10.25 to 12, that is 0.854 - inside the 0.78 to 0.92 band.

Window heights follow at 0.82-0.88 measured; 5/6 = 0.833 by Palladio's rule, compounding by storey. The measured band and Palladio's rule agree to within two per cent, which is the reason to trust either.

correct_practice: Each storey is about 0.85 of the one below it measured floor to floor, and the window heights follow at 0.82-0.88. On a 10 ft first storey that is 10 ft 0 in and 8 ft 6 in, with a dormer or attic window at about 41 in. Italianate graduates harder - an 11 to 14 ft first floor diminishing 8 to 15 per cent per storey. The purpose is structural legibility, not decoration: the graduation is what makes a front sit on the ground rather than float, because the eye reads the heavier, taller element as the supporting one.

fixes.right: Two stud lengths and two window sizes. A 10 ft first storey and an 8 ft 6 in second, with the second-floor sash one light row shorter.
fixes.cheap: If the storey heights cannot move, graduate the WINDOWS. Hold both head heights where the ceilings put them and shorten the second-floor sash by one row of lights - 9/6 below and 6/6 above, or a taller and a shorter 6/6. This recovers most of the visual effect for the price of a different window unit, which in a mixed order is often zero, and it is exactly what the pattern books did.
fixes.dishonest: Shortening the second-floor windows by dropping the HEAD rather than raising the sill. The head heights are the datum that the cornice and the door head belong to; a dropped head produces a band of blank wall under the cornice and reads as a mistake, whereas a raised sill reads as a smaller room, which is what it is.

test.note: The measured band, and Palladio's 5/6 = 0.833 sits inside it - they agree to within two per cent, which is the reason to trust either. The fault reads 0.98-1.02. This needs no scale reference because it is a ratio between two objects in the same image.

secondary_tests.note: storey-graduation gives 0.85; facade-classical's invariant gives 10.25:12 = 0.854. Read off the water table, belt course and cornice where they exist.
The attic ratio, which is what sizes a dormer window at about 41 in on a 10 ft storey.

detection: In a straight-on photograph, measure the sash height of a first-floor window and of the sash directly above it. A ratio of 0.82-0.88 is correct; 0.98-1.02 is the fault. Second, read the floor-to-floor heights off the water table, belt course and cornice where they exist. Third and fastest, at any distance: if the upper and lower windows are visibly the same unit, the graduation has gone.

exceptions.why: The principal floor is the SECOND floor at 12-13 ft, taller than the ground floor at 10-11 ft, which inverts the rule and is correct: the piano nobile is upstairs, away from the street, the damp and the heat.
exceptions.bounds: The ground storey must read as a base and the storey above the principal floor must diminish again to 10-11 ft. The inversion is between the first two floors only.

bounds_test.note: The ground storey must read as a base and the storey ABOVE the principal floor must diminish again to 10-11 ft. The inversion is between the first two floors only.

granted_when.note: Depends on the vertical social section and the piazza, not on the style label.

exceptions.why: Same logic - the principal floor is raised above a service or flood level, and it is the tallest.
exceptions.bounds: The raised base must be expressed as a base: piers, an arcade, or a low service storey with smaller openings.

bounds_test.note: The raised base must be expressed as a base: piers, an arcade, or a low service storey with smaller openings.

exceptions.why: The frieze-band attic collapses the top storey into a band of the entablature, which is a graduation so extreme it becomes a different rule.
exceptions.bounds: The storey below must still be full height, and the band must be a frieze with horizontal windows in it, not a knee wall of siding.

bounds_test.note: The storey below must still be full height, and the band must be a frieze with horizontal windows in it, not a knee wall of siding.

granted_when.note: Confined to a habitable half-storey lit within the entablature.

exceptions.why: Ceiling heights are differentiated by FUNCTION - 6 ft 10 in to 7 ft 4 in at compression, 9 ft 0 in to 10 ft 0 in at release - rather than by storey, so a Prairie house may legitimately have a taller upper volume.
exceptions.bounds: The differentiation must be legible outside as a change in the horizontal banding, not merely felt inside.

bounds_test.note: The differentiation must be legible outside as a change in the horizontal banding, not merely felt inside.

exceptions.why: Graduates MORE, not less: 8-15 per cent per storey off an 11-14 ft first floor.
exceptions.bounds: Not an exception to the rule but an intensification of it.

bounds_test.note: Not an exception to the rule but an intensification of it.

inverted_by.statement: Downward graduation between the first two storeys is the fault. The principal floor is the SECOND at 12-13 ft over a ground floor of 10-11 ft, because the piano nobile is upstairs away from the street, the damp and the heat.
As above - the principal floor is raised above a service or flood level and is the tallest.
As above, over a rusticated basement reached by an exterior stair.

confused_with.difference: That is the same axis pushed past zero into inversion. Equal storeys are inert; an inverted pair is actively unstable.
That fault is about the height of a single plate on a type whose defining measurement is that plate. This one is about the relation of two full storeys of windows to each other.

sources: Andrea Palladio, I quattro libri (1570), Book I on the diminution of storeys
